text: Sixty-six million years ago, the most powerful animals on Earth vanished.
And the killer came from space.
But what really happened? And did every dinosaur truly disappear?
Dinosaurs ruled the planet for about one hundred sixty-five million years.
Our own species has existed for only around three hundred thousand years.
So how could such a successful group fall so fast?
The first clue was hidden in rock.
In nineteen eighty, a team led by Luis and Walter Alvarez studied a thin layer of clay that marks the end of the dinosaur era.
It was full of iridium, a metal that is rare on Earth's surface, but common in asteroids.
The impact site was found later, buried under Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula.
It is called Chicxulub, a crater about one hundred eighty kilometers wide.
The asteroid that made it was roughly ten kilometers across. Wider than Mount Everest is tall.
The impact triggered giant tsunamis, powerful earthquakes, and huge wildfires.
But the deadliest part came next.
Dust, soot, and sulfur were thrown high into the sky, and they blocked much of the sunlight.
For months, and maybe years, the planet became darker and colder.
Scientists call this an impact winter.
Without enough sunlight, plants struggled to grow.
Plant eaters starved, and then the meat eaters that hunted them.
In the end, about three quarters of all plant and animal species disappeared.
The asteroid may not have acted alone.
Around the same time, giant volcanic eruptions in India, called the Deccan Traps, released huge amounts of gas.
Scientists still debate how much they contributed. But the asteroid is seen as the main trigger.
Here is the twist: not all dinosaurs died.
Birds are the descendants of small feathered dinosaurs. So, in a way, dinosaurs still live among us.
The pigeon in the park is a distant relative of Tyrannosaurus rex.
Small animals that could burrow, hide, or eat almost anything had a better chance.
Among the survivors were small mammals. With the giants gone, they spread across the world.
Millions of years later, one of their branches led to us.
The dinosaurs were not slow or weak. They were simply unlucky.
